relativeScale.name: Major Scale
relativeScale.intervalDistance: Half step above the Locrian root (B Locrian = C Major)

keyExamples.notes: B - C - D - E - F - G - A - B
keyExamples.commonUse: Most common Locrian key, parent scale is C major, natural starting point for learning the mode

keyExamples.notes: F# - G - A - B - C - D - E - F#
keyExamples.commonUse: Popular for metal riffs on drop-tuned guitars, parent scale is G major

keyExamples.notes: E - F - G - A - B♭ - C - D - E
keyExamples.commonUse: Open string root for extremely dark guitar riffs and dissonant passages

keyExamples.notes: A - B♭ - C - D - E♭ - F - G - A
keyExamples.commonUse: Jazz contexts over half-diminished chords and avant-garde compositions

patterns.description: Root on 6th string 7th fret, the diminished 5th (F natural) creates the unstable, tense characteristic Locrian sound.
Open string root on E with the flat 5th creating maximum tension against the open string resonance.
Low position pattern starting on the 2nd fret, useful for heavy drop-tuned metal riffing and djent patterns.

commonPositions.usage: Metal riffs, diminished-based solos, dissonant passages
Doom metal, experimental guitar, dark atmospheres

diatonicChords.function: Tonic - Diminished tonic chord, inherently unstable and restless, the defining feature of Locrian
Supertonic - Major flat-II, provides a strong contrast to the diminished tonic
Mediant - Minor chord offering relative stability within the unstable mode
Subdominant - Standard minor subdominant providing some grounding
Dominant - Major chord built on the characteristic diminished 5th degree
Submediant - Major chord for harmonic color and brief moments of brightness
Subtonic - Minor subtonic chord, common resolution target within the mode

commonProgressions.name: Locrian Drone (i°-♭II)
commonProgressions.description: The fundamental Locrian movement - the diminished tonic pulling toward the major flat-II creates maximum tension and instability

commonProgressions.name: Locrian Descent (i°-♭vii-♭VI-♭V)
commonProgressions.description: Descending chromatic-flavored progression exploiting the dark dissonance of Locrian for extreme tension and dread

commonProgressions.name: Dissonant Metal (i°-♭II-♭iii-i°)
commonProgressions.description: Metal-style progression cycling through the most accessible Locrian chords before returning to the unstable diminished tonic

genreApplications.usage: Provides the darkest, most dissonant tonality available within the standard modal system for extreme heaviness
Sophisticated dissonance over half-diminished (m7b5) chords and experimental harmonic textures
Creates dread, unease, and psychological tension through diminished instability and unresolved dissonance

practiceExercises.name: B Locrian Scale Runs
practiceExercises.description: Practice the B Locrian scale ascending and descending, focusing on the characteristic flat 2nd and diminished 5th intervals
instructions: Start slowly with metronome at 60 BPM
Listen for the diminished 5th (F natural) that makes Locrian uniquely dark and unstable
Compare with B natural minor to hear the flat 2nd and flat 5th differences

practiceExercises.name: Locrian Tritone Emphasis Drill
practiceExercises.description: Isolate and practice the root-to-flat-5th tritone interval that defines the Locrian mode's instability and darkness
instructions: Play the B to F interval repeatedly to internalize the tritone tension
Approach the tritone from different scale degrees to hear it in context
Practice resolving the tritone outward (B down to Bb, F up to F#) to understand its pull

practiceExercises.name: Locrian vs Phrygian Ear Training
practiceExercises.description: Compare Locrian with Phrygian mode to isolate the diminished 5th that distinguishes Locrian as the darkest standard mode
instructions: Play B Locrian, then B Phrygian back to back
Focus on the 5th degree difference (F natural vs F# in B)
Notice how the diminished 5th removes all sense of tonal stability

relatedScales.differences: Phrygian has a perfect 5th instead of diminished 5th - Locrian is Phrygian with a flatted 5th
relatedScales.usage: Dark and exotic but more stable than Locrian due to the perfect 5th

relatedScales.differences: Aeolian has a natural 2nd and perfect 5th; Locrian flattens both for maximum darkness
relatedScales.usage: Common minor mode with full tonal stability, much less dissonant than Locrian

relatedScales.differences: Symmetrical 8-note scale vs 7-note Locrian; both exploit diminished harmony but with different structures
relatedScales.usage: Jazz and metal contexts requiring diminished sounds with more note options

prerequisites: All other modes of the major scale
Understanding of diminished harmony and the tritone interval
